title: Electrical, battery and fuel safety
audience: Field workers, crew leaders and supervisors on outdoor and garden sites who use corded or battery tools, generators, petrol engines and fuel containers.
learningOutcomes: Identify electrical, battery and fuel hazards on a garden or outdoor site before starting work.
Inspect corded tools, extension leads, battery packs and fuel containers and remove defective items from service.
Refuel and store petrol engines and batteries using the controls in this lesson.
Stop work and refer any mains wiring, fixed electrical or gas task to a licensed tradesperson.

instruction.heading: What this lesson covers and what it does not
instruction.body: Outdoor work brings electricity, batteries and fuel into wet, uneven and crowded places. A mower lead can be cut by a spade, a battery pack can overheat in a hot ute, and a petrol can left beside a running trimmer is a fire waiting to happen. This lesson teaches you to recognise those hazards, apply the controls that a worker is allowed to apply, and stop and refer everything else. It does not authorise you to install, repair, rewire or connect any fixed electrical installation, irrigation controller mains supply, outdoor lighting circuit or gas appliance. Those tasks need a licensed electrician or other licence holder under the rules that apply in your state or territory. Finishing this lesson does not give you a licence, a certificate or authority to do regulated electrical or gas work. Check {{business:compliance.licence_requirements}} before any task that goes beyond inspecting and reporting.

instruction.heading: Recognise electrical hazards on site
instruction.body: Start every job by looking at the power supply before you plug anything in. Look for outlets without protective covers, boards placed on wet grass or bare soil, and leads that cross paths, gates or driveways where vehicles run over them. Check each extension lead for cut or nicked insulation, exposed copper, cracked plugs, heat marks, and connectors that have been taped together. A lead that works is not automatically a safe lead. Where your tools or outlets are supplied with residual current device (RCD) protection, confirm that it is present and working using the test button before use. Where a site has no RCD protection and you are not sure whether the outlet is protected, do not assume it is. Stop, use a tool that is known to be protected, and ask your supervisor. Treat any buried or overhead cable you cannot identify as live until a competent person confirms otherwise. Work near overhead power lines, and tree work above a set height or near lines, is outside this business and needs the licensing that applies to it.

instruction.heading: Batteries, chargers and fuel
instruction.body: Lithium-ion battery packs used in blowers, trimmers and mowers store a lot of energy. Damage can cause overheating, swelling, smoke or fire. Inspect each pack before use. A pack that is cracked, leaking, swollen, hot to touch or smells unusual must come out of service. Do not charge a damaged pack, do not drop it into a bin, and move it to a clear, non-combustible area away from fuel and dry vegetation. Charge only with the charger supplied for that battery and at a location that is cool, dry and ventilated. Do not charge a hot battery straight after heavy use. Petrol and two-stroke fuel need separate handling. Store fuel only in approved containers that are clearly labelled, away from ignition sources and out of direct sun. Refuel engines only when they are switched off and cool. Wipe up spills before starting the engine. Never refuel a running engine, and never smoke near fuel. Petrol engines in enclosed or poorly ventilated spaces produce carbon monoxide, so do not run them in sheds, garages or under covered areas without fresh air.

instruction.heading: Controls, isolation and when to stop
instruction.body: Use the hierarchy of control. The first choice is to avoid the hazard, for example by using a battery tool where it is suitable instead of a long extension lead. Next, substitute a safer tool or fuel system. Then separate people from the hazard, for example by keeping leads out of the walking path and out of the cutting zone. Only after those steps should you rely on PPE, such as eye protection, hearing protection and gloves that suit the task. Before adjusting, clearing a jam or changing a blade, switch the tool off, remove the battery or unplug it, and wait for moving parts to stop. Keep cords clear of blades and wheels, and never run a cord through standing water or under a wet tarp. Stop work immediately if a tool trips its RCD repeatedly, if a lead becomes warm, if you smell burning or if fuel leaks. Tell your supervisor, make the area safe and record the event. Do not attempt to fix a fault in fixed wiring, a switchboard or a garden lighting circuit yourself.

instruction.heading: Verification and escalation
instruction.body: A supervisor should check what you do, not only what you can describe. During a site check, you should be able to point to the defective item, explain why it is unsafe, show the correct removal from service and name the person you would inform. The pass evidence is an inspection record for each tool, lead and battery, with photographs taken with consent showing any defect and its isolation. Escalate immediately to the supervisor for any exposed wiring, any shock, any fuel leak near an ignition source, any swollen or smoking battery, and any electrical fault in fixed wiring or a controller. Where the fault involves mains supply, the decision to repair belongs to a licensed electrician, not to the crew.

procedure: Confirm the task is inspection, isolation and safe storage, and that no fixed electrical or gas work is part of the job.
Identify every power source, battery and fuel container on the site and mark the routes the cords and fuel will take.
Inspect each extension lead, plug and tool cord for damage and remove any defective item from service with a clear tag.
Check that the outlet or board is RCD protected where the site or equipment requires it, and test the RCD before use.
Inspect each battery pack and charger for swelling, cracks, heat or leaking; set aside any damaged pack in a clear, non-combustible location.
Store fuel in labelled approved containers away from ignition sources and direct sun, and refuel only with the engine off and cool.
Wipe up spills, check the work area for trip and fire risks, and keep cords out of the cutting zone.
Stop work and inform the supervisor when any hazard cannot be controlled. Record what you found, what you isolated and who you informed.

workedExamples.situation: A crew arrives at a backyard to clear a garden bed. The trimmer lead is cut through near the fence, and the outlet on the back veranda has no cover and sits in a puddle.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do with the trimmer, the lead and the outlet, and who do you tell?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not use the cut lead and do not tape it. Remove the trimmer from service and stop using that outlet while it is wet and uncovered. Use a battery tool or a protected outlet that is known to be safe if the task allows. Tell the supervisor and the customer that the outlet needs a licensed electrician to inspect and repair. Record the defect and the isolation, and photograph the defect only with the customer's consent.

workedExamples.situation: During a hot afternoon a battery blower feels hot and a crew member notices the battery casing is bulging.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the safe sequence for the battery and the equipment?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop using the blower and remove the battery. Move the battery to a clear, non-combustible area away from fuel, dry leaves and vehicles, and keep people back from it. Do not charge it and do not place it in a bin. Tell the supervisor, follow the manufacturer's and the business's procedure for damaged batteries, and record the event. A swollen battery is a damaged battery, even if it still works.

equipmentAndPpe: RCD test device or built-in RCD test button, where fitted
Approved, labelled fuel containers with spill tray
Fire extinguisher suitable for petrol and electrical fires, as specified in the site plan
Non-combustible storage container for damaged batteries
Eye protection and hearing protection suitable for the tool in use
Gloves suitable for handling fuel and handling blades

commonErrors.error: Using a cut or taped extension lead because the tool still runs.
commonErrors.prevention: A lead with damaged insulation is removed from service. Repair of mains supply leads and connectors is not a crew task. Tag the lead and tell the supervisor.

commonErrors.error: Refuelling a hot or running engine, or spilling fuel and starting the engine straight away.
commonErrors.prevention: Switch off and allow the engine to cool before refuelling. Wipe spills and check for leaks before starting.

commonErrors.error: Charging a swollen or hot battery because the job is urgent.
commonErrors.prevention: Damaged packs come out of service. Charging waits until the battery has been assessed under the business's procedure.

commonErrors.error: Reading this lesson as permission to fix a fault in a controller, switchboard or garden light.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop at inspection and referral. Name the licensed electrician or licence holder who must carry out the work, and record the referral.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson covers inspection, isolation and referral only. It does not authorise electrical, gas or fixed-wiring work, and it does not grant an electrical licence or any authority to do regulated work.
Electrical work licensing differs between states and territories.

Overhead power lines are a serious electrocution hazard. Safe Work Australia's general guide sets the no-go zone around overhead electric lines as one that no one may enter without written approval from the electricity supply authority, and it says distances for other zones depend on a written risk assessment.

The model Work Health and Safety framework requires duty holders to eliminate risks so far as is reasonably practicable and to work through the hierarchy of control measures for certain risks. PPE is the lowest level of control.
Check the applicable state or territory rule and the tool manufacturer's instructions.

qualityStandard: Every corded tool, lead and battery used on the job has been inspected before use and recorded.
No defective lead, plug or battery is used, and each defective item is removed from service with a visible tag.
Fuel is stored in approved, labelled containers, and refuelling is done with the engine off and cool.
Any mains wiring, fixed electrical or gas defect has been referred to a licence holder and the referral has been recorded.
documentationEvidence: Pre-start inspection record for leads, plugs, tools and batteries, with the date, the worker's name and the result.
Record of any item removed from service, including the defect, the isolation and the person informed.
Referral record for any electrical, gas or fixed-wiring defect, with the customer's notification.
Photographs of defects taken with the customer's consent, with personal information removed.
summary: Electrical, battery and fuel hazards are common in outdoor work, and a damaged item is removed from service rather than repaired on site.
Refuel only with the engine off and cool, and store fuel in approved containers away from ignition sources.
A swollen or hot battery is a damaged battery. Do not charge it.
Any mains wiring or fixed electrical fault is referred to a licence holder. This lesson does not grant a licence.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker finds a garden extension lead with a cut in the outer sheath and exposed copper. What is the correct action?
options: Wrap the cut with electrical tape and continue, because the tool still runs.
Use it only at low speed, because the cut is short.
Remove the lead from service, tag it, inform the supervisor and record the defect.

knowledgeChecks.question: When is it safe to refuel a petrol-powered trimmer?
options: When the engine is switched off and has cooled, with no ignition sources nearby.
While the engine is still warm, so it restarts quickly and the cap is left open
Whenever the fuel can is sealed, even if the engine is running and the area is clear

knowledgeChecks.question: A battery pack for a blower is bulging and warm. Which action is correct?
options: Charge it at a slow rate to cool it down before using it again and then check it again later
Remove it from use, move it to a clear non-combustible area and report it under the business procedure.
Place it in the green-waste bin so it is collected with the clippings on the same day

Zone B approach distances are based on a written risk assessment. Publisher: Safe Work Australia. The guide is dated July 2014; its current status has not been confirmed. officialReferences.title: Identify, assess and control hazards: managing risks
officialReferences.covers: Removing a risk is the best control. Where a risk cannot be eliminated, it must be reduced so far as is reasonably practicable. Control measures are listed from strongest to weakest, and administrative controls and PPE are described as the least effective. Publisher: Safe Work Australia.
